metadata.title: Measuring mathematics competence in international and national large scale assessments_ Linking PISA and the national educational panel study in Germany

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses a Germany-based linking design combining PISA 2012 mathematics (administered to 9th graders via a single group design) and NEPS mathematics for grade 9 (NEPS-K9). The analytic dataset comprises 1,678 students who took the PISA mathematics test booklet on day 1 and 1,330 students who took the NEPS mathematics test on day 2, with 1,270 students taking both tests; the sample is drawn from 78 secondary schools (80 classes) within five German federal states and stratified by school type. The manuscript does not report the use of complex survey weights (e.g., student design weights) or any replicate-weight procedure; therefore, weighting is not documented as part of the estimation. Scoring relies on Rasch/WLE transformations and then equipercentile linking (LEGS 2.01) with cubic-spline smoothing, rather than on ML model estimation that would typically require survey-weighted inference.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: This paper is a scale-linking and comparability study that maps NEPS mathematics scores to the PISA 2012 mathematics scale using Rasch/WLE scoring and equipercentile linking. The dependent quantities are linked scale scores and proﬁciency-level classifications derived from those linked scores, not PV-based cognitive achievement outcomes in the sense of PISA plausible values. Missing-data handling is not described because the analysis focuses on linking functions and descriptive/comparative statistics for the linking study sample rather than on an ML pipeline with explicit missingness procedures.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Linking study in Germany (spring/summer 2012) using a single group design at schools participating in a school development program. On day 1, each student completed one PISA 2012 mathematics test booklet; on day 2, the same students completed NEPS mathematics tests for 9th graders (NEPS-K9). Only five of the 13 PISA booklets were used, selected for having the most mathematics (and science) items. The realized dataset includes 1,678 9th graders who took the PISA mathematics test and 1,330 ninth graders who took the NEPS mathematics test; analyses reported for the linking and comparability results use the subset of 1,270 students who took both mathematics tests. The sample is drawn from within five German federal states, stratified by school type, with an approximate class participation rate of 79%.

main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2012 the study leveraged the reported predictors to predict Literature synthesis outcome (not student-level prediction), finding that This study evaluates how NEPS grade-9 mathematics can be related to PISA 2012 mathematics by establishing a concordance between the two scales. Data come from a Germany-based linking study (spring/summer 2012) where 9th graders completed PISA 2012 mathematics on day 1 and NEPS-K9 mathematics on day 2; only five PISA booklets were used, and the reported linking analyses rely on the 1,270 students who took both tests. PISA mathematics was scored using Rasch with fixed item parameters and transformed to the international PISA 2012 achievement scale metric via WLE; NEPS mathematics was scored with a Rasch model using fixed item parameters from NEPS 2010 and WLE person separation reliability around 0.791–0.796. The linking function was created using equipercentile linking in LEGS 2.01 with cubic-spline smoothing (slim = 0.5). Results show substantial correlation between PISA and NEPS scores (manifest r = 0.68; latent ≈ 0.90), close reproduction of PISA score-equivalent distributional characteristics, and fair individual-level classification consistency (Cohen’s Kappa ≈ 0.26), with limitations including an unmodeled order effect and reduced exactness at score extremes. This indicates that these patterns have implications for educational policy and instructional practice, though cross-sectional ILSA designs cannot establish causality.

data.null_fields_interpretation: The paper is not an empirical machine-learning prediction study; it is a measurement-linking and comparability study. Consequently, there are no ML algorithms to extract, no PV-handling strategy for PV-based achievement modeling, and no ML target-variable performance metrics (e.g., AUC/RMSE) to report. The main empirical outputs are linking-function results (equipercentile concordance), score distribution comparisons, correlations, and classification consistency statistics.
